sources.entry: Bounded rationality: rational individuals will select a decision that is satisfactory rather than optimal

summary.title: Bounded rationality - Wikipedia
summary.one_liner: Bounded rationality holds that people, limited by problem difficulty, cognitive capacity and time, choose satisfactory (satisficing) decisions rather than optimal ones.
keywords: why people don't make optimal decisions
limits of human rationality in economics
takeaways: Bounded rationality says decision-makers are limited by problem difficulty, cognitive capacity and available time, so they settle for satisfactory options (satisficing).
Herbert A. Simon coined the term as an alternative to the globally rational 'economic man' assumed in neoclassical economics.
Heuristics such as availability, representativeness and anchoring-and-adjustment are presented as ways people cope with these limits, sometimes producing biased judgments.
Related concepts include nudging, bounded willpower, bounded selfishness, rational inattention, and Gigerenzer's ecological rationality and adaptive toolbox.
The page notes the idea is applied across political science, economics, psychology, law, philosophy and cognitive science.
summary.summary: This Wikipedia article defines bounded rationality as the idea that limited problem difficulty, cognitive capacity and time lead people to choose satisfactory rather than optimal decisions. It traces the concept to Herbert A. Simon as a replacement for global rationality in economic modelling, and covers heuristics (availability, representativeness, anchoring), Gigerenzer's adaptive toolbox and ecological rationality, and behavioral economics ideas such as nudging, bounded willpower and bounded selfishness. It also summarizes Kahneman and Tversky's psychology work and lists related articles and references. The page is a general overview with a number of sections flagged as needing citations or possibly containing original research.
